questions.question: Describe a spur gear and explain what the terms driver, driven and gear train mean, using the mealie grinder as an example.
questions.expected_answer: A spur gear is a wheel with straight teeth around its rim that interlock with the teeth of another gear so the two cannot slip. The driver gear is the one the effort is applied to (the gear on the handle shaft of the grinder); the driven gear is the one turned by the driver (the gear on the grinding shaft). Two or more meshing gears together form a gear train. Teeth must be the same size to mesh, and we count teeth rather than measure diameter.

questions.question: State the rule of counter-rotation and explain why meshing gears obey it.
questions.expected_answer: Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions. At the point where the teeth touch, both teeth move the same way, but that point is on the right of one gear's centre and on the left of the other's, so the same movement is clockwise for one gear and anticlockwise for the other. Along a straight train the direction alternates with every gear.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of an idler gear, what it does and does not change, and why it is often made of a harder material.
questions.expected_answer: An idler sits between the driver and driven gears and meshes with both. Its mesh adds a second reversal, so driver and driven turn the same way; with equal driver and driven gears they turn at the same speed in synchronisation. The idler does not change the speed or force ratio, which depends only on the driver and driven gears, and it can be any size, which also lets the designer bridge a gap between shafts. Because it meshes on two sides it wears faster, so it is often made of harder material such as steel.
